name: simd-radix-sort (SIMD MSB radix sort with separate key and payload streams)
baseline: std::sort (STLSort in the thesis); thesis also compares Intel IPP Radix Sort, Bramas AVX-512 quicksort, Blacher AVX2 quicksort and Moeller's SIMD radix sort
workload: Sorting 2^18 elements, time per element, int32 keys with uniform distribution (also int32 key plus int32 payload, and double keys with Gaussian distribution), AVX-512 build.
claimed_speedup: Thesis Figure 8.16 (int32, Uniform): RadixSIMD 10.16 ns/element vs STLSort 41.87 ns/element (about 4.1x, derived from page data). Figure 8.17 (int32-int32): 11.19 vs 41.94 ns/element (about 3.7x, derived). Figure 8.18 (double, Gaussian): 16.33 vs 44.71 ns/element (about 2.7x, derived). Not the fastest: on int32 Uniform IPPRadix 5.55, BramasSort 3.62 and BlacherSort 2.45 ns/element are all faster than RadixSIMD.
hardware: Intel Core i7-12700K at 5 GHz, 32 GB RAM, Manjaro Linux kernel 5.17.15 (AVX-512 enabled; thesis notes Intel does not officially support AVX-512 on Alder Lake)
tradeoffs: x86-64 only and needs AVX-512 F/BW/DQ/VL/VBMI/VBMI2 (the single header must be compiled with those flags); C++20; generic over key and payload types; sorts keys and payload streams separately.
caveats: Bachelor's thesis benchmark, authors' own harness (src/perf-thesis.cpp, results written to /tmp). libstdc++ is implied by gcc on Linux, not stated. Cross-algorithm comparison covers only 2^18 elements. The library is slower than IPPRadix, BramasSort and BlacherSort on the shown cases (its own thesis says most time is spent in the comparison sorter). README says a quicksort variant gave similar performance and was not published as a paper. Intel IPP rows need the proprietary IPP library.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/avx512?l=c%2B%2B page 3 listing; thesis PDF fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com and read with pdftotext

name: Ultra-Sort (SIMD sorting DSL for AVX2 and AVX-512)
workload: Sorting 2^20 (1M) elements of 32-bit and 64-bit ints and floats and key-value pairs, single core, wall time in seconds; also a 1024-element table and a 10M-element AVX2 table.
claimed_speedup: Project report Table 4 (1M elements, 32-bit int): avx512::sort 0.010364 s vs std::sort 0.080234 s (about 7.7x, derived from page data), ips4o 0.035442 s, pdqsort 0.036089 s, avx256::sort 0.019070 s. Report abstract: best-case speedup of 8x on single-core and 17x on multicore AVX-512. At 1024 elements (Table 7) avx512::sort is 5.69x std::sort for 32-bit int.
compiler_and_flags: Report: 'compile with flag -O3 -flto'; CMakeLists: -g -O3 -flto -Wall -march=native -fopenmp; compiler vendor and version not stated
hardware: Intel Xeon Silver 4114 at 2.20 GHz, 40 logical CPUs, L3 14080 KB (Skylake-SP, AVX-512)
tradeoffs: x86-64 AVX2 or AVX-512 only; element count must be a power of two (README); built for course-project scale, no NUMA support; single-thread SIMD sort, optional OpenMP multicore.
caveats: Course-project report, not peer reviewed; README speedup chart is an image (not opened); numbers here come from the report PDF in the repo. Compiler name and version missing, so one step short of tier A. Gains are uneven: 64-bit key-value int avx512::sort (0.106933 s) is slower than std::sort (0.085 s) at 1M elements, and the 10M-element AVX2 int table shows only 1.5x. ips4o, pdqsort and std::stable_sort are in the same tables for context.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/avx2?l=c%2B%2B page 2 listing (PatwinchIR/ultra-sort); README links the report; reports/ProjectReport.pdf read with pdftotext

name: PQ Fast Scan
baseline: PQ Scan (product quantization distance scan with lookup tables in L1 cache; the project's own reference implementation, also with SSE, AVX and AVX gather variants)
workload: Nearest-neighbour scan of product-quantized vector codes: distance lookup tables kept in SIMD registers instead of the L1 cache, exact same results as PQ Scan.
claimed_speedup: README: 'PQ Fast Scan to perform 4-6x faster than PQ Scan, while returning the exact same results' (chart image not readable here).
compiler_and_flags: g++ 4.9.x recommended ('benchmarked it with this version only'); build flags in CMakeLists not opened
tradeoffs: Needs SSE2/SSE3/SSSE3 and POPCNT; relies on reorganising code lists, which prevents combining it with inverted indexes (README); Linux with libpfm4; best results only with g++ 4.9.
caveats: Tier B rests on the peer-reviewed PVLDB paper cited in the README (Andre, Kermarrec, Le Scouarnec); the paper could not be opened (vldb.org blocked), so the 4-6x figure is quoted from the README. README states no CPU model. The same README's pqscan output shows that SSE and AVX variants of plain PQ Scan are not faster than the scalar scan, so the gain is from the algorithm. Clear BSD has no patent grant and is not listed by OSI (permissive, treated as copyable).

name: Quick ADC
baseline: ADC (asymmetric distance computation in product quantization, lookup tables in L1 cache; the authors' scalar implementation)
workload: Nearest-neighbour search over product-quantized codes using 4-bit quantizers so lookup tables fit SIMD registers (AVX/AVX2 scan_avx_4), batches of 32 queries, with inverted-index support.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Quick ADC achieves 4-6x better performance than ADC by storing lookup tables in SIMD registers'.
compiler_and_flags: g++ 5.4 or newer, sequential (single-threaded) BLAS, OpenCV core, Cereal 1.2.2; flags not opened
hardware: Tested on Intel Haswell, Broadwell and Skylake processors (README); exact CPU model for the speedup chart not stated
tradeoffs: Needs AVX2 (Haswell or newer); 4-bit quantizers cause 'a slight decrease in accuracy' (README says often negligible); builds on the same idea as PQ Fast Scan.
caveats: Tier B rests on the peer-reviewed ICMR 2017 paper cited in the README; the paper (ACM and arXiv) could not be opened here, so the 4-6x figure is quoted from the README and the chart is an image on a blocked host. Baseline ADC is the authors' own implementation. Clear BSD has no patent grant and is not listed by OSI (permissive, treated as copyable).
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/simd?l=c%2B%2B page 7 listing (technicolor-research/quick-adc); README of technicolor-research/pq-fast-scan also links it

name: pospopcnt_avx512 (positional popcount benchmark, AVX-512BW Harvey-Seal)
baseline: scalar positional population count (pospopcnt_u16_scalar in the same repo)
workload: Positional popcount over a 19.073 MB array of 16-bit words (n = 10,000,000, 100 iterations), cycles per 16-bit word and GB/s.
claimed_speedup: Sample output: pospopcnt_u16_scalar 17.325 cycles per 16-bit word (0.367 GB/s) vs pospopcnt_u16_avx512bw_harvey_seal_1KB 0.497 cycles per word (12.407 GB/s), about 35x (derived from page data); 512B and 256B variants 0.538 and 0.618 cycles per word.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: -O3 -march=native, -std=c99 for C and -std=c++0x for C++; compiler name and version not stated in the sample output
hardware: 'a Cannon Lake processor' (sample output, estimated clock about 3.1 GHz); exact model not stated
tradeoffs: Requires AVX512BW hardware (Cannon Lake, Ice Lake and newer, Zen 4); Linux with bare-metal perf-counter access recommended; the repo also carries a Go-style assembly benchmark (golike_benchmark).
caveats: Companion repo of the paper by Klarqvist, Mula and Lemire (CCPE 2021, arXiv 1911.02696); the paper was not opened (arXiv blocked). Covers the same technique as mklarqvist/positional-popcount, which is already catalogued, so it may fold into that entry. Single sample run on one machine, scalar baseline is the authors' own loop.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github SIMD AVX-512 vpcompress OR vpermb OR left pack OR prefix sum OR histogram C++ library benchmark vs scalar' surfaced lemire/pospopcnt_avx512 (via awesome.ecosyste.ms)

name: bilinear_filter_simd
baseline: plain scalar C++ bilinear filter in the same repo ('No SIMD')
workload: Bilinear downscale of a 3840x2160 image to 1280x720 with SSE4, AVX2 and AVX-512 kernels, single-thread and multi-thread, Google Benchmark.
claimed_speedup: README, Xeon Platinum 8124M, single thread: No SIMD 13.3 ms, SSE4 10.7 ms, AVX2 8.14 ms, AVX512 7.33 ms (1.24x, 1.63x, 1.81x, derived from page data); multi-thread 1.25 ms vs 0.822 ms AVX512 (1.5x derived). Core i7-8700 single thread: 7.64 ms vs SSE4 5.26 ms vs AVX2 4.26 ms (1.8x derived). Benchmarks.md (2020-08-11 run): AVX512 single thread 5.87 ms vs 13.3 ms.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release (default optimisation level), -march=native, C++17; README says GCC >= 8; exact compiler version not stated (Dockerfile uses ubuntu:23.04 build-essential)
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8124M @ 3.00 GHz (16 threads) and Intel Core i7-8700 @ 3.20 GHz
tradeoffs: x86-64 only (SSE4, AVX2, AVX-512 paths); needs OpenCV 4 as a dependency of the demo; multithreading helps more than SIMD in the shown results.
caveats: No licence file in the repo, so the code is reference only. Benchmarks are from 2020 and the repo is a demo. Baseline 'No SIMD' is the author's scalar code built with -march=native, so compiler auto-vectorisation of the baseline is possible. SIMD gains are modest (1.2x to 2.3x single-thread) and small in the multi-thread case.

name: SIMD-math-prims (vectorizable approximate sin, cos, log, exp)
baseline: libm sinf, cosf, logf, expf (scalar single-precision functions)
workload: Single-precision sin and cos on [-3.14159, 3.14159], log on [1e-10, 10], exp on [-10, 10], throughput in million evaluations per second, compared against libm and with error statistics.
claimed_speedup: README output: sinf 213.3M/s vs sinapprox 6238.5M/s (about 29x); cosf 226.7M/s vs cosapprox 7380.7M/s (about 33x); logf 115.2M/s vs logapprox 4112.9M/s (about 36x); expf 111.3M/s vs expapprox 2366.8M/s (about 21x) (ratios derived from page data). README text: 'speedups from 20x to 40x' with gcc vectorisation.
compiler_and_flags: README: gcc or clang with -O3 -march=native (auto-vectorisation); versions not stated
tradeoffs: Approximate: sin mean absolute error 3.7e-6, cos 2.6e-5, log 5.6e-6 (README output); header-only and portable but relies on compiler auto-vectorisation, so speedups depend on gcc or clang loop vectorisation.
caveats: Output is 'on my computer' with no CPU or compiler version. The speedup is mostly from vectorising an approximation over a loop versus calling scalar libm (precision trade-off, no accuracy-matched comparison). Not intrinsics-based despite the category, so it is closest to a vectorisable-math library. Numbers also appear in the mipac fork's README (identical).
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'SIMD vectorized math library exp log sin cos AVX2 AVX-512 faster than libm' surfaced mipac/SIMD-math-prims, a fork; canonical repo is jhjourdan/SIMD-math-prims

name: vectorized_find (AVX2 find experiments)
baseline: std::find on a raw array and on std::vector (plus a naive loop)
workload: Worst-case search (target at the end) over 4096 int elements, Google Benchmark, billions of elements per second.
claimed_speedup: README table: FIND_CppFind ~7.7 G-elements/s and FIND_CppVectorFind ~8.1 G-elements/s vs FIND_IntrinsicFind ~24.9 (about 3.2x vs raw-array std::find, derived from page data) and FIND_IntrinsicFloatFind ~25.3; FIND_Intrinsic2Find ~49.7 (about 6.5x derived); naive loop ~4.6.
compiler_and_flags: CMakeLists: GCC -mtune=native -march=native -mavx2 -Ofast -funroll-loops -ftree-vectorize; Clang -O3 -ffast-math ...; compiler used for the table not stated
tradeoffs: AVX2 only; fixed 4096-element size in the quoted table; Intrinsic2Find has lower_bound semantics on a sorted array rather than a plain find.
caveats: Personal experiment with no licence file and no hardware stated (docs/perf_results text files exist; the part of results.txt read shows no CPU header). Intrinsic2Find counts elements below the target on a sorted array, so the 49.7 figure is a different algorithm from std::find. Std::find is measured with -Ofast flags in CMake. Rounded numbers ('~').

name: SIMD_TriangleAABB (SIMD triangle-box overlap test)
baseline: Moeller's scalar triangle-box overlap code ('old code', and the 'new, faster code' variant) from Tomas Akenine-Moeller's page
workload: Triangle-vs-AABB overlap tests in four scenarios (best case, worst case, no hit, mixed), time in the program's own units, SSE implementation with an extra early exit.
claimed_speedup: README, vs Version1 (old code): best case 20.617886x, worst case 1.987882x, no hit 2.896657x, mixed 3.295337x; vs Version2: 26.198313x, 2.587267x, 4.126582x, 3.375974x. Times: default 5072/3773/953/5088 vs optimized 246/1898/329/1544.
hardware: 'my test PC' (Windows-based machine, CPU not stated)
tradeoffs: SSE (128-bit) code; keeps branches and early exits instead of branchless SIMD; theoretical maximum from 4-wide SIMD is 4x, the 20x best case comes from an added early exit.
caveats: Numbers are from the README text copy of the 2021 blog post, with no compiler, flags or CPU stated. No licence file (author asks for a tip jar), so code is reference only. The 20x best case is the extra 'box contains triangle' early exit, not SIMD throughput; typical gain is 2x to 3x (author says so). The author reports other SIMD versions of the same test that were slower than the original.

name: vstat (SIMD descriptive statistics on EVE)
baseline: Boost.Accumulators 1.69, GNU Scientific Library 2.6, NumPy 1.19.4 and linasm statistics 1.13
workload: Variance (univariate) and covariance (bivariate) of 1M uniform random float and double values, data size increased in 100k steps, nanobench ops per second.
claimed_speedup: Plots only (no numeric table). Read off the 'Variance double' log-scale plot at 1M elements: vstat about 4e9 op/s, linasm about 4e9 op/s, Boost.Accumulators about 2.5e8, NumPy about 1.5e8, GSL about 8e7, so roughly 16x Boost, 27x NumPy, 50x GSL, and parity with linasm (approximate, read from plot, not page text).
tradeoffs: C++20; built on the EVE SIMD library (itself catalogued); header-only; data-parallel Youngs-Cramer sums combined with Schubert-Gertz; scalar accumulators available when no SIMD type is used.
caveats: README gives methodology and CPU but no compiler, flags or numeric table; the four PNG plots are the only results and the figures above are approximate readings of the log-scale axes. vstat only ties linasm on variance. MKL was not used for NumPy and GSL (README note), and linasm needs precomputed means that were included in its timing.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/simd?l=c%2B%2B page 8 listing (heal-research/vstat, built on EVE)

name: IntrinsicML (hand-vectorized SIMD microkernels for ML)
baseline: plain triple-loop scalar C++ reference (GCC -O3 -ffast-math); also OpenBLAS sgemm single thread (where it is slower)
workload: Single-precision GEMM (packed AVX2/AVX-512 kernel) at 64x64 to 512x512, and GeLU on 1M elements, single core.
claimed_speedup: README table: GEMM 64x64 about 0.7x (slower than scalar), 128x128 about 10x, 256x256 about 26x vs scalar; GeLU 1M elements about 6-10x. Versus OpenBLAS (1 thread) the kernel reaches only about 4% (64), 29% (128), 55% (256), 59% (512). docs/BENCHMARKS.md CI run: 4-8x over scalar.
compiler_and_flags: README: both compiled with -O3 -ffast-math; docs/BENCHMARKS.md: GCC-12, -O3 -march=native -mfma -ffast-math, Ubuntu 22.04
hardware: Virtualised x86-64 CI runner with AVX2+FMA, about 2.1 GHz calibrated TSC, exact model varies (docs/BENCHMARKS.md)
tradeoffs: Needs AVX2 + FMA (AVX-512 kernel auto-dispatched); educational middle ground between textbook loops and production BLAS; Python bindings via pybind11.
caveats: Honestly slower than OpenBLAS and slower than a scalar loop at 64x64 (the author explains GCC auto-vectorises the reference). Numbers come from noisy shared CI VMs; the README's 10x and 26x differ from the 4-8x in docs/BENCHMARKS.md, and the preprint was not opened. Scalar baseline is built with -ffast-math, so it can be auto-vectorised.

name: recip_rsqrt_benchmark (fast vectorized reciprocal and rsqrt)
baseline: exact IEEE SSE reciprocal and square-root variants in the same repo (recip_*_ieee, rsqrt_*_ieee: division and square-root instructions)
workload: Vectorized 1/x and 1/sqrt(x) on 4 floats or 2 doubles with rcpps/rsqrtps plus optional Newton-Raphson refinement; CPU cycles per call and maximal relative error.
claimed_speedup: README sample results (float4): recip ieee 7.30 cycles vs fast 1.13 (about 6.5x, max error 3.0e-4) vs nr1 3.69 (about 2.0x, error 1.47e-7); rsqrt ieee 14.46 vs fast 1.12 (about 12.9x, error 3.3e-4) vs nr1 5.52 (about 2.6x, error 3.1e-7); double2 rsqrt ieee 28.21 vs fast 3.38 (about 8.3x) (ratios derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 2013 C++ compiler, x64 mode; optimisation flags not stated in README
stars_or_usage: 11 stars; tied to a Stack Overflow answer
tradeoffs: Approximate results (error trade-off listed per variant); SSE on x86 only; benchmark of approximate rcpps/rsqrtps tricks rather than a packaged library.
caveats: No licence file, so reference only. Old measurements on Ivy Bridge with MSVC 2013; newer CPUs have faster divps and sqrtps instructions (general knowledge, not from the page), so the gap is likely smaller today. The 'ieee' baseline is the authors' own exact variant in the same harness.

name: optimize-cnn (hand-written NEON tiny CNN inference)
baseline: ONNX Runtime 1.27.1, ncnn 20260526 and TensorFlow Lite 2.20.0 (tuned by the author)
workload: Inference of a tiny Fashion-MNIST CNN over 70,000 images with 4 threads, best of N runs, wall time.
claimed_speedup: README table: cnn_fuse 783 ms and cnn_neon 1045 ms vs cnn_ort 2440 ms, cnn_ncnn 2302 ms, cnn_tflite 1621 ms (cnn_fuse about 3.1x vs ORT, 2.9x vs ncnn, 2.1x vs TFLite, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build, C++17, OpenMP; compiler name and version not stated
hardware: Raspberry Pi 4B (4x Cortex-A72 at 1.8 GHz, 4 GB RAM)
tradeoffs: Hard-coded model architecture and fixed hardware (Cortex-A72 NEON, fused conv-pool-activation kernels); not a general inference framework.
caveats: Machine-learning inference rather than a general SIMD library, so the category may be wrong. Model is tiny and fixed, the author tunes the framework baselines, and compiler and flags are not stated, so the tier stays at C even though benchmark code and hardware are public. Uses the author's hand-written GEMM from optimize-gemm (already catalogued).

name: fast-bernoulli (AVX Bernoulli sampler with LLVM JIT)
baseline: std::bernoulli_distribution-style sampler ('Std' sampler, thresholding a uniform draw)
workload: Generating blocks of Bernoulli-distributed bits with a given probability using logical operators on random words, AVX and JIT-compiled samplers, Google Benchmark with parameter 128.
claimed_speedup: README Google Benchmark table: BM_StdSampler/128 72,260,140 ns (55.395 k/s) vs BM_AvxSampler/128 71,017 ns (55.0 M/s) vs BM_JitAvxSampler/128 55,667 ns (70.2 M/s); about 1000x and 1300x by time (derived from page data); BM_GenericSampler/128 104,076 ns.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build, C++17; compiler and version not stated
hardware: 4 x 3400 MHz CPUs, L1d 32K, L2 256K, L3 4096K (Google Benchmark header); model not stated
tradeoffs: Returns bit-packed blocks rather than bools; probability is quantised into a sequence of AND and NOT operations; uses AVX vectors and optional LLVM JIT; Python bindings.
caveats: Table units for the Std sampler (k/s) and AVX sampler (M/s) differ and the amount of work per iteration is not obviously equal, so the roughly 1000x gap may reflect bit-packed output versus one bool per sample. Compiler and CPU model missing. Random-number-generation baseline row (4786 ns) shows RNG cost alone is far below the Std sampler time.
